text:
ARTEX

 Autonomous penetration testing that keeps its receipts. 

(upstream: Autumn-27/ARTEX, AGPL-3.0)

Self-hosted multi-agent offensive security. A planner explores, workers run real tools,
and every finding stays bound to the assets and HTTP traffic that prove it.

 
 
 
 

Quick start · Screenshots · How it works · Install · Configuration · Security

 

---

ARTEX is a self-hosted, LLM-driven penetration testing platform. It is not a chat wrapper around
a scanner: a planner splits a goal into intents, workers execute them with real tools, and the
results are written back into two linked graphs : one for what you know about the target, one
for how the test is progressing. Every finding can carry the captured request and response that
justify it, and every autonomous action passes through scope rules, approval gates and budgets.

- It explores, it doesn't chat. Goal decomposition, intent dispatch, worker execution and
 write-back form a closed loop that keeps advancing until the goal is proven.
- Two graphs, one audit trail. The shared asset graph says what exists ; the per-task
 exploration graph says what was tried, what it produced, and why . Anchors link the two.
- Findings with evidence. A recording MITM proxy and a browser extension capture real traffic;
 findings, evidence quotes and retests are tied to the exact request/response.
- Autonomy with brakes. Human-in-the-loop approvals, argv-prefix rules, scope/deny gates,
 token and turn budgets, a target noise governor, and prompt-injection framing on tool output.
- Self-hosted and model-agnostic. One Go binary with the Next.js UI embedded, PostgreSQL,
 your own Anthropic/OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or a local Ollama.

---

 Multi-provider workers

In System → LLM , configure the profiles you want to use. In System → Settings ,
set the concurrent worker count to at least 2 before starting a task (the count
applies to subsequently started tasks). In System → Agents → Worker , leave the
model set to follow the task; a fixed Worker model takes precedence over rotation.

When creating a task, select both profiles in LLM config chain , arrange their
order, and enable Enable multi-LLM worker rotation . For an existing task, open
its LLM config control, change the switch or profile order, and save.

Rotation assigns successive worker intents A, B, A, B, regardless of completion
order. Separate intents can run concurrently on different providers; each intent
keeps its selected provider unless it fails over. Planner and other unbound roles
continue using the task's current profile. Turning rotation off restores ordered
task-level failover. An excluded provider is skipped, so an intent pinned to an
exhausted profile falls back to the task's current profile instead of retrying it;
rotation keeps cycling the whole list and does not rebalance around a dead provider.
Saving the chain resets their failure state. Changes do not interrupt in-flight
calls. The rotation cursor starts again after a server restart and saving the chain
does not reset it; the profile order and switch remain persisted.

The task creation and PUT /api/tasks/{id}/llm APIs accept llm rotate: true alongside
the ordered llm profile ids . Omitting llm rotate on an update preserves its value.

---

 How it works

 Dual-graph architecture: exploration graph + asset graph

ARTEX separates what the goals are from how far testing has progressed into two independent
graphs linked by anchors:

- Asset graph (shared across tasks). One source of truth for root domain / subdomain / ip /
 service / app / endpoint , owned by companies. Parent-child relationships and deduplication keys
 are computed by the program; agents only submit raw observations.
- Exploration graph (per task). The task's reasoning and progress: goal / intent / fact /
 finding / hint nodes connected by spawns / derived from / yields / proves edges into a lineage
 chain.
- Anchors link them. exploration anchors(node id, asset id) ties intents, facts and findings
 to concrete assets: which assets a direction touched, and which intents tested a given asset.
 This also powers asset test coverage and the coverage graph.

 

The planner reads the exploration graph, judges goals, and dispatches intents only when there
is an uncovered direction; a worker claims one intent, executes it, writes assets/facts/findings
back into both graphs, then stops.

 The engine loop

The engine is event-driven: any graph change wakes the planner, workers claim and execute intents,
write-back triggers the next round, until prove goal closes the task.

 

 Durable attack chains, shared worker memory

Real attack chains are multi-step and ordered (find an injection → get credentials → move
laterally). The planner keeps a todolist retained per task across wake-ups : it records the
chain once, then dispatches the next step only when its prerequisites are satisfied by facts.

Workers can also search each other's execution traces ( search all worker traces ,
 list worker traces , get worker trace ). Observations that never became formal facts (an error
message, a response snippet, a hidden parameter) are still reusable by the next worker, while each
worker remains confined to the intent it claimed.

---

- Recording MITM proxy ( :8788 )

install.title: Quick start
install.html:
git clone https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX.git
cd ARTEX
cp .env.example .env            # set POSTGRES_PASSWORD (and optionally an LLM key)
docker compose up -d --build    # builds from this checkout, starts PostgreSQL

Open http://localhost:8787. On the first visit /setup asks for the one-time setup token printed at startup:

docker compose logs artex | grep "Setup token"

There is no prebuilt Docker image to pull: the image is always built from your checkout. For all installation paths (script, binaries, source, release archives), see Installation.

features.title: Features
features.html:
Evidence, not chat logs

  • Recording MITM proxy (:8788) with a generated CA: every Bash/HTTP tool call is traced, and request/response evidence can be bound to a finding.

  • Browser extension (extension/) for authenticated targets: log in once (captcha, email OTP, 2FA included), capture the session, and the requests/responses land in the same traffic store.

    Using the traffic capture extension
    • Load the unpacked extension from extension/ (Chrome/Edge: Developer Mode → Load unpacked);
    • In the popup, set your ARTEX URL and token, then press Start capture on the tab you are browsing;
    • Use the site normally; text requests/responses are batched to POST /api/traffic/ingest (authenticated). Binary bodies (images, fonts) are skipped, bodies are truncated at 256 KiB, batches are capped at 50 entries;
    • Press Stop when done. Everything stays in your local traffic store.

  • Verified findings: findings carry a POE level, a verification status and a note; a finding is verified only when a bound proof/response and verbatim evidence quotes support it. Gzip/deflate bodies are decoded before the quote check.

  • Vulnerability retest loop: a dedicated retester agent re-runs a finding with optional fixed version/conditions, records Still reproducible / Fixed / Cannot confirm, and can move the finding to Fixed automatically. Original evidence and reports are preserved.

  • Reports and exports: findings, evidence and task archives, with traffic snapshots kept encrypted at rest.

Control without slowing down
  • Interception gate: every tool call can require human approval, with rules by string, regex or argv prefix. An argv rule is a JSON array of 1 to 8 tokens (Bash only, for example ["git","push"]); it matches only a single simple command whose parsed prefix equals the pattern exactly. Pipes, lists, redirections, prefix assignments, subshells, background jobs, wrapper programs and command/parameter substitutions do not match; flags are ignored by construction (["git","push"] covers git push --force, but git -C /repo push matches nothing). Each approval records who decided: human, rule, model or system.
  • Scope and target gate: scope rows define the coverage denominator; assets outside the declared scope are not explored. The target gate (off by default, API-only) can refuse destinations that were not approved.
  • Budgets: ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TOKENS / ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TURNS cap a whole task (planner and workers); ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TOKENS / ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TURNS cap one worker run. Near the limit the task enters a forced wrap-up; a worker is not started when the remaining budget cannot cover it. Budgets are in memory: a restart starts fresh.
  • Noise governor: ARTEX_NOISE_PROFILE=quiet|balanced|aggressive paces requests ARTEX sends to targets (per-host rate, burst, in-flight limit, jitter, backoff on 429/503, short GET caching). With a profile set, agents also receive low-and-slow flags for the installed scanners.
  • Untrusted-output boundary (on by default): tool results are framed between nonce-tagged markers so the model treats them as data, not instructions. Disable with ARTEX_UNTRUSTED_BOUNDARY=0.
Assets and coverage

  • Coverage ledger and force-directed coverage graph: in-scope assets are highlighted as tested or untested, with linked intents, facts and findings per node.

  • Company-scoped asset graph: shared across tasks, deduplicated by the program, with domain → subdomain → service → endpoint containment.

  • ScopeSentry sync: pull asset data from a ScopeSentry instance by project or task, merged by company scope into the asset graph for agents to explore.

    Syncing from ScopeSentry
    • On the Asset Sync page, enter the ScopeSentry address and API key;
    • Choose the targets and asset types by project or task (domains / subdomains / IPs / ports / sites / endpoints…);
    • Import: rows are merged by company asset scope and become part of the asset graph.

  • Task categories, templates, relations and archives for repeatable engagements.

Platform
  • LLM profiles with failover: Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenAI-compatible relays and keyless Ollama; multiple profiles per task with automatic failover.
  • Token accounting: per-task and per-session usage, cache reads/writes, and an LLM record view for every call.
  • MCP servers, skills, memory and a workspace: extend the agent with remote tools and reusable prompt/playbook material.
  • Single binary: the Next.js UI is embedded with go:embed; PostgreSQL is the only external dependency.
